### A request for AI company staff [[00:00:00]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-company-staff-reprioritise?t=0)

**Rob Wiblin:** I have a request of all AI company staff: reflect today on whether the project you’re working on is the best thing you can plausibly be doing to either delay [recursive self-improvement](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement) (RSI) or make it go well. And if it’s not, push to be moved to an alternative project _you think_ is more valuable.

Obviously many staff are already trying hard to do exactly that. But the strategic situation is changing incredibly quickly, so if you aren’t asking yourself the hardest questions regularly and being honest about it, there’s a growing risk you’ll accidentally be wasting your time.

On the technical side there are a few lines of work that stand out as especially likely to remain relevant up to RSI:

*   Work that solves fundamental problems in [alignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment), obviously
*   Work that gets current models to better pursue alignment research today
*   And work that ensures we can catch, understand, and announce model misbehaviour or misuse as early as possible

By contrast, some work that looks suspicious to me includes:

*   Any alignment methods that throw band-aids on existing issues, but which can’t scale to the models that will be engaging in recursive self-improvement
*   Anything that has the practical effect of making underlying alignment problems less visible to the public and policymakers — without simultaneously fixing the drives causing the behaviour
*   Anything that primarily improves model capabilities — especially the ability of models to autonomously do AI R&D
*   And anything that’s primarily about attracting customers, or achieving commercial advantage

I appreciate that these prioritisation decisions are extremely difficult and complex. Already in these two short lists there’s a clear tension:

*   On the one hand I think it’s valuable to get today’s models to more vigorously and sincerely help with [technical alignment research](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-technical-research/).
*   On the other hand, I’m wary of alignment methods that work today but won’t work tomorrow, and of anything that makes AIs better at AI R&D — even though many types of AI alignment research are extremely close to AI R&D.

That’s why neither I nor anybody else can do this prioritisation for you. You have access to experimental results we don’t. And you can sensibly ask yourself questions like: “Is my work doing more to assist with getting useful alignment research out of today’s models, or doing more to shorten timelines to RSI?” in a way nobody far away from your particular situation can do.

I also know that for almost all of you, this is not going to be the first time someone has prompted you to make these tradeoffs better. But with things as chaotic as they are, it can be easy to slip into working on something that’s not especially impactful, or even harmful.

For instance:

*   Maybe you’re working on a project you started a year ago, when you thought RSI might first become possible in 2029. Now you think recursive self-improvement will become possible in 2027 most likely, and your current work doesn’t seem likely to be relevant by then. But that shift in timelines hasn’t yet flowed through to a change in your work.
*   Maybe you’ve gotten more safety-pilled this year, by [Mythos](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/claude-mythos-hacking-alignment/) and [Hugging Face](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/hugging-face-hack/) and all the rest. But you haven’t yet made the hard decision that requires you to work on something substantially different.
*   Maybe you’ve been so rushed fighting fires and shipping models the last three months that you haven’t had a single afternoon to reflect on what your high-level priorities ought to be.
*   Maybe you think there are more important projects, but what you’re currently doing is what your manager wants, and pushing for something else feels awkward, difficult.
*   Maybe you’ve invested a year in a promising project and gotten real results from it. But you’re increasingly unsure whether it deserves a second year, and giving up partway through would be unpleasant.

These are all incredibly human and relatable things we’ve all done. And in a situation that weren’t so incredibly dangerous and urgent, we’d leave people to reassess when they’re ready to do so. But as it is, there’s no time for that.

Not being at a frontier company myself, there’s a lot of confidential information I lack. But to give you some ideas, here’s how some priorities appear to have shifted to me.

For this purpose, I’m going to take it as given that the internal models inside Anthropic and OpenAI are much more powerful again than [Opus 5.5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5) and [Astra](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra), and that OpenAI has seen alignment on its unreleased models go backwards. And in keeping with the [dominant attitude within frontier companies](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/), I’m taking it as given that fully automating AI R&D may become possible in 2027, 2028, or 2029.

### Chain of thought [[00:03:34]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-company-staff-reprioritise?t=214)

As I discussed [last time](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-takeover-soon-oversight-monitorability/), [OpenAI has reported](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra) that the effectiveness of chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring on its models is dropping precipitously. [Google has now reported the same](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/gemini/gemini_4_safety_report.pdf) with its latest model, [Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-argon/).

This trend has various implications:

*   [Chain-of-thought monitoring and analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11473) today is absolutely still useful inasmuch as it helps us to identify, understand, publicise, and respond to misbehaviour sooner. Only finding out about rogue AIs months after they happen robs us of time to react.
*   But chain-of-thought monitoring will only scale to the beginning of recursive self-improvement if we can find ways to reduce what models can accomplish without a chain of thought, or keep models honest and forthcoming on that chain of thought.

If you’re working on chain-of-thought monitorability as a strategy, you have to ask yourself if you think those things are going to happen. Opus 5.5 doesn’t have the same ability to control what it writes in its chain of thought, so maybe it can be done. If you believe that will work, keep going and maybe pitch in to make it work. If not, it’s time to reprioritise.

The increasing problems with monitorability are also an update in favour of [white-box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_box_%28software_engineering%29) monitoring techniques like [mech interp](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/neel-nanda-mechanistic-interpretability/), over [black-box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_box) ones like CoT monitoring.

Separately, I think they’re also an update in favour of making recursive depth or no-CoT capabilities a regulatory target. That’s a story for another day.

### Don’t paint over the cracks [[00:04:44]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-company-staff-reprioritise?t=284)

Imagine that you’re responsible for building maintenance on a large apartment block. People keep complaining about cracks appearing in an outer wall, and paint and plaster falling down on top of them. You do a walk around the building and realise that this isn’t just a superficial problem with the outer wall. The building has a problem with its foundation that’s leading half of it to subside, and the cracks are just a sign of that deeper issue. Over time the subsidence will likely get worse and eventually become actually dangerous.

Like anyone, you’ve only got limited time and money. There’s four things you might do:

1.   Do nothing about either problem.
2.   Repaint the wall but do nothing about the foundation.
3.   Alternatively, let the visible cracks stay, and prioritise fixing the underlying issue.
4.   Or finally, both repaint the wall and fix the foundation.

Now, there’s nothing wrong per se with painting over cracks and repairing plaster. High-quality building maintenance is going to do both.

But the underlying problem with the foundation is obviously far more important. If you only have resources to do one of the two, you fix the foundation that could lead the building to collapse, not the surface issue that’s merely aesthetic, and the thing that allowed you to notice the problem in the first place.

And if you know the foundation is not on track to be repaired, painting over the cracks in the wall so externally things look fine — that’s a sort of deception on the residents.

Don’t be cajoled or peer-pressured into participating in an effort that only makes a risk harder to see, rather than actually reduces it.

### It may not be your most aligned model ever [[00:06:00]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-company-staff-reprioritise?t=360)

Every time a model card comes out now, labs effectively say, “Our safety evals look better than ever” — but then also say in slightly more technical language, “We trust our safety evals less than ever.”

That’s for many reasons, including [eval awareness](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/marius-hobbhahn-ai-scheming-deception/), ability to scheme off the chain of thought, and the risk of having effectively [trained on the test set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leakage_%28machine_learning%29).

I’m glad that reality isn’t being covered up. But if you’re working on safety evals you suspect now misinform people as much as they inform, ask what it would take to make them truly credible again:

*   Scenarios the model actually can’t tell apart from real use
*   Methods of directly suppressing eval awareness
*   Or maybe something new I’ve never heard of

If your work is helping restore credibility so you really believe your safety evals, great. If not, in my view it’s time to reassess and probably find something more useful to do.

### Capabilities advances look worse [[00:06:44]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-company-staff-reprioritise?t=404)

However good or bad it was in the past, as we get closer to recursive self-improvement and to [superintelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence), work that improves AI capabilities looks less attractive than it used to.

That’s for a number of reasons:

1.   Today’s models are closer to the models you plan to hand over AI R&D to, and so which pose the gravest risks. That means we have more relevant [model organisms](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/ChDH335ckdvpxXaXX/model-organisms-of-misalignment-the-case-for-a-new-pillar-of-1) to study and improve, without needing to improve capabilities further.
2.   The models we have now are actually able to make really useful contributions to all kinds of technical alignment work, and even policy and governance work sometimes. The more we can draw things out, the more time we have to exploit that assistance.
3.   The later things get, the less time there is remaining for any [career capital](https://80000hours.org/articles/career-capital/) you accumulate in the course of improving AI capabilities to pay off and more than compensate for any damage done.
4.   Existing internal models are smart enough for most business applications now, so one can potentially have a flourishing AI business by making them better and cheaper and more aligned products for enterprise customers, rather than pushing them closer to superintelligence.
5.   Capability advances beyond what internal models can already do now pose [actual catastrophic risks](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-extinction-explained/) primarily now via [bio misuse](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026#biological-misuse-sep-26), or models [silently compromising AI company systems](https://www.anthropic.com/news/investigating-incidents-cybersecurity-evals).

Doing capabilities research at an unusually reckless lab is just extremely difficult to defend at this point. If you work at a company you think has the world’s best safety practices, though, I know the [steelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man#Steelmanning): if the most careful lab isn’t at the frontier, someone else more reckless will be.

And it’s a reasonable point. But two things are gradually eroding its persuasiveness over time:

*   Firstly, breakthroughs are leaking to less careful actors very quickly now via [distillation](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-251a), [espionage](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-security/), and poaching of staff. So a lead is harder than ever to maintain.
*   And second, the frontier we’re approaching is now automated AI research itself. Getting there first only helps if the careful lab can tell whether it’s possible to do it safely, and if so, how. And today, nobody can.

That’s why we have to [pace the frontier](https://www.pacingthefrontier.com/).

And it’s also why, if you’ve been striking one tradeoff between ‘increasing capabilities’ against ‘other impacts,’ it’s necessary to recalculate and double-check if what you’re doing still really makes sense.

### Ever less need for altruists to do commercially focused work [[00:08:50]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-company-staff-reprioritise?t=530)

This shift has been going on for years, but all the frontier AI companies are huge commercial enterprises now. Many people working at all of them are thinking of them primarily as businesses, and their job is to figure out how to attract customers and build better products. The commercial incentives to do that kind of work are enormous, because it brings in a lot more revenue than it costs.

If you’re motivated primarily by reducing catastrophic risks, and you’re primarily working on improving products or the customer experience, you should think hard about whether that’s actually the greatest contribution you could be making. I think typically, in your absence, the company would get similar results from somebody else, while you could be doing much more important and neglected safety and alignment and governance work.

### Pacing the frontier [[00:09:29]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-company-staff-reprioritise?t=569)

We’ve gotten to the point where AI capabilities are truly dangerous without solving alignment. We tried to avoid that for many years by waking up the world sooner, and sadly we’ve failed.

If we just continue to barrel forward, improving capabilities faster than alignment — or, heaven help us, proceed to fully automate AI R&D with safety cases as weak as the ones we possess today — the [risk of human extinction](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RIJJB5B2lHU) is terrifyingly high.

That means most good futures now run through scenarios where we somehow succeed at pacing the frontier, to buy ourselves a couple of years for automated alignment research and [data centre security](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/infosecurity-compilation/) and the law and so on to catch up.

Many actors can contribute to that effort:

*   There’s only a few relevant companies at the moment, so we only need a handful of companies to voluntarily limit the types of RSI they engage in to begin buying time. [OpenAI’s Safety and Security Committee](https://openai.com/index/openai-board-forms-safety-and-security-committee/) could potentially step in and object to dangerous research practices at OpenAI, for example.
*   California might contribute some useful laws in a [special session](https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/09/ai-rules-newsom-state-directive/) that they might hold in November and December.
*   And if the problem gets even more obvious, a new Congress might act decisively as soon as next year — whether or not the president tries to veto it.
*   If Congress doesn’t act, public outrage might be necessary to force their hand. But if the problems are obvious enough I think that’s actually pretty realistic, given [how the public feels about AI](https://apnorc.org/projects/most-adults-think-ai-is-developing-too-fast/) even now.
*   And such pacing arrangements would soon have to extend to China, which will require [credible technical demonstrations](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/daniel-kokotajlo-ai-2040-plan-a/) of why they’re necessary, and all the rest of it.

As you know, the [Overton window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overton_window) here has shifted enormously in the last two months. So if you’ve been working on something other than pacing the frontier, but you think one of the steps above is something you could make a big difference to, you should reassess and decide if that might now be your greatest opportunity for impact.

### Organising staff [[00:11:07]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-company-staff-reprioritise?t=667)

Changing projects is something you can do on your own. But you may be able to have even more leverage acting as a group. If you’re on the technical staff, you have extraordinary bargaining power. You can slow things down simply by not taking part. You can leave for other impactful, well-paid work. And when you speak up, the public takes you far more seriously than outsiders like me.

But your influence within the company only lasts so long as your employer needs you, and you’re building the machine researchers designed to make you obsolete. Once that happens, you’ll lose much of your ability to direct events. So if this power is going to be used, it has to be used ASAP.

If staff at OpenAI and Anthropic simply refused to keep walking us closer to the cliff edge, that could be the first of several mechanisms that let us pace the frontier. In practice, that might mean pushing for limits on how far and how fast AI R&D gets automated; or insisting on credible, independent safety assessments before dangerous thresholds are crossed; or demanding a way to take serious concerns all the way to the board without any risk of retaliation.

This approach actually sidesteps a problem the companies face, and helps them out in one respect: an agreement between lab leaders to slow down runs into [antitrust law](https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/09/ai-pacing-agreements-legal-issues-and-how-to-attempt-to-manage-them). But staff pressing their own employer to slow down as a matter of personal conscience don’t have that problem.

The hard part is usually that nobody wants to be the one to go first, which is why [agreements that only kick in once some critical threshold has been reached](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assurance_contract) might help out.

You will know far better than me how much any of this is realistic, but maybe somebody listening is in a position to help get the ball rolling on this. One group already working on this is the [Coalition of Concerned AI Staff](https://concernedaistaff.org/), which launched earlier this year to help staff act on their beliefs as a group.

### Consider working somewhere else [[00:12:38]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-company-staff-reprioritise?t=758)

Alternatively, your best opportunity might not be at the organisation you currently work for.

[We recently interviewed Geoffrey Irving](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/geoffrey-irving-superintelligence-alignment-theory/) about the new organisation he’s cofounding: [Resolution](https://resolution.org/).

They’re working to two- to three-year timelines to superintelligence, scaling up incredibly fast, and aiming to tackle neglected bets in alignment that can plausibly continue working through to recursive self-improvement, and perhaps beyond.

The primary mechanism will be automating the research — that is to say, guiding AIs through doing it for us. And their approaches are more formal and mathematical than what AI companies are doing, so now that AI is basically in the process of solving mathematics for us, it’s easier to see those lines of work paying off. It’s extremely compute intensive, but if they make early progress I think they’re very likely to get access to the billions in compute that they’ll need to make the full project work.

[Listen to our interview with Geoffrey](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/geoffrey-irving-superintelligence-alignment-theory/) if you want to learn more. And if you don’t feel amazing about what you’re doing now, consider [applying there](https://jobs.80000hours.org/?refinementList%5Bcompany_data%5D%5B0%5D=Resolution&jb_source=podcast__episodes__ai-company-staff-reprioritise) or to [another group doing outstanding work](https://jobs.80000hours.org/?jb_source=podcast__episodes__ai-company-staff-reprioritise) outside the leading companies.

### Reprioritise [[00:13:27]](http://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-company-staff-reprioritise?t=807)

The above was just my current best guess based on what I see not being at a frontier company. I’m sure some of it is wrong, and if you do think some of it is misguided or misinformed in some specific way, I’d sincerely like to hear — drop me an email at [rob@80000hours.org](mailto:rob@80000hours.org).

I’m sure many of you have reprioritised and been bold about changing what you’re working on in recent months. But if you haven’t gotten to that yet, there’s no time like tonight.

Take 20 minutes. Write down in a few sentences how your current project makes RSI go better or come later. Is it focused on a sensible target? Will it pay off in time? If you walked away, would the company find someone else to do a similar job to what you’re already doing? What else could you do that you suspect might be even more impactful? Then show your answers to someone you respect and ask them for a candid opinion.

We all wish this weren’t happening in our time. At least I definitely do. But sadly that’s not for us to decide. All we have to decide is what to do with the unfortunately brief time that is given us.

And on that note, I’ll speak with you again soon.

title: The age of initiative
content:
We’re unprepared.

In high school, the quarterback isn’t allowed to call the plays, the actor isn’t allowed to write the lines and the math whiz isn’t allowed to choose what to prove.

We all grew up in the age of compliance (and indoctrination).

The long tail of the internet and the astonishing leverage of AI has made this training much less valuable.

No matter what you do for a living, there’s a machine standing by, waiting for instructions. Instructions from you, if you choose, or from your overlords if you don’t.

And following the playbook isn’t much help, because the world is changing so fast, a playbook is obsolete by the time someone hands it to you.

One reason AI got such a fast start is that it gave people seeking compliance a chance to wait for the AI to tell them what to do next. Quick, cheap answers.

AI gives bosses a cheaper (and often more compliant) alternative to hiring humans to do some tasks.

For those indoctrinated to comply, this is stressful. The stress is due to a desire to get things back to normal, to give them a chance to comply again, but right here, right now, is as normal as things are ever going to get. “Good jobs” are no longer sinecures where success comes from following instructions.

It’s an abrupt change, and winging it is insufficient. Handling this sudden transition alone is too difficult. But we have a chance to find the others, to connect and be part of a [cohort](https://seths.blog/2026/10/purple-space-problem-solving/) that challenges, educates and encourages each other on the path to find a way forward.

We accepted that it was required to spend years being trained to handle a life of compliance. Now we have the chance to lean into the hard work we’ll need to do to thrive in an age of initiative.

title: The Surprising Origins of Native Hawaiians
content:
Hawaii is one of the most isolated islands on Earth, surrounded by vast oceans for thousands of miles on every side. And yet humans have been living there for nearly a millennia. They’re part of the Polynesian diaspora. This culture of ultravoyagers embarked on their own age of exploration while Europe was still mired in the Middle Ages, colonizing the tiny islands dotting the South Pacific without the benefit of metal tools, navigational equipment, or a written language. Now, a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/science.aec7662) in _Science Advances_ is better defining their genetic history.

“What we uncover in this paper is where the Native people of Hawaii had come from,” study author Alexander Ioannidis of Stanford University said in a [statement](https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2026/10/hawaiian-genetics.html). “Hawaii is the only Polynesian island in the Northern Hemisphere, so it’s a long way from everything.”

**Read more: “**[**Hawaii’s False Killer Whales Are Wasting Away**](https://nautil.us/hawaiis-false-killer-whales-are-wasting-away-1281866)**”**

After excavating the genomes of Native Hawaiians for clues, Ioannidis and a team of geneticists and anthropologists were able to track their origins some 4,400 miles away to Easter Island. Previous genetic research conducted by the team allowed them to look even further back in time, retracing the path of the diaspora that eventually wound up in Hawaii. Polynesian peoples spread to Fiji and Tonga, then pushed east to the Cook Islands, Tahiti, and Mangareva. They settled on Easter Island in the early 1200s, but they didn’t stop there.

According to the team, generations of island-hopping left their mark on the genomes of these ultravoyagers, especially the Native Hawaiians at the end of the line. When a smaller subsection of a population settles in a new place, the founders of the new colony only carry a fraction of the population’s gene pool. The result is a genetic bottleneck (called the founder’s effect) that can magnify the frequency of previously rare genes in the following generations, turning uncommon alleles into common ones.

The team determined that founding populations grew rapidly following settlement, preventing the new gene pool from being swamped by future migration. Additionally, because the genomes of Native Hawaiians passed through chains of these bottlenecks en route to their final destination, it compounded the founder’s effects.

“By the time you’ve gotten all the way to Hawaii, you’re at the end of a series of founder effects, so it’s really intense,” Ioannidis explained. “What we discovered is in the Eastern Polynesians, such as Native Hawaiians, the founder effects are more than an order of magnitude, so more than 10 times, larger than what we have in the populations of European descent we’ve studied so well.”

These European bottlenecked populations (including the Finnish and the Amish) have slightly elevated risks of developing certain genetic disorders, and Native Hawaiians are no different. The team identified three deleterious alleles that occur at a slightly higher frequency (between 2-4 percent), which cause conditions like dislocated lens in the eyes, vision loss, and kidney failure.

According to the researchers, it’s a problem that needs to be addressed. “We don’t have recommendations for genetic testing, and there’s no reimbursement from insurance because these are conditions we don’t even know about,” Ioannidis said. “This is a population that should be getting research resources and attention from geneticists even more urgently.”

Their ancestors conquered the oceans using nothing more than what grew on their islands and an oral navigation tradition, it’s the least we can do. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How Crocodiles Survived the Asteroid That Killed the Dinosaurs
content:
Dinosaurs and crocodilians popped up around the same time roughly 245 million years ago, but only one group survived the asteroid impact 65 million years ago (avian dinosaurs, aside). But why? According to a new study published in _Science Advances_, the secret of crocodile success boils down to three things: location, location, location.

A team of researchers led by paleontologists from University College London examined over 7,000 fossils and records belonging to more than 400 species (living and dead) from pseudosuchia, a larger group that includes crocodilians. They then compared the records to computer models reconstructing Earth’s changing climate over the past 245 million years to map out the global history of the group across space and time.

**Read more: “**[**This Ancient Crocodile Ancestor Learned to Walk on Two Legs**](https://nautil.us/this-ancient-crocodile-ancestor-learned-to-walk-on-two-legs-1278684)**”**

With a couple notable exceptions, the team found that crocodiles survived by moving to warmer climes. When Earth’s temperature was around 18 degrees Fahrenheit warmer as recently as 50 million years ago, the reptiles ranged as far north as Europe and Antarctica. After a period of global cooling, they retreated to the tropics, where they thrive today.

The researchers also focused on how climatic changes immediately after the asteroid impact may have affected crocodilians. Using models to simulate the chilly temperatures resulting from sunlight-blocking clouds of dust, the team tested a few different scenarios. With sunlight dimmed by five or ten percent, crocodiles still prospered in equatorial regions, they found, but turning the dimmer switch down to 15 percent proved to be too chilly for the cold-blooded reptiles.

“These findings have implications for species today,” study author Philip Mannion of University College of London said in a statement. “If crocodiles mostly coped with past climate change by moving towards suitable habitats, today’s species will need room to move as the planet warms, and the loss of suitable areas to roads, farms, and cities is making that harder.”

It’s worth pointing out that while crocodiles may have survived the mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs, they didn’t survive unscathed. Earth was once home to a panoply of pseudosuchian diversity—there were [long-legged terrestrial crocs](https://nautil.us/newly-discovered-prehistoric-crocodilian-had-legs-that-went-all-the-way-up-1268721), massive 40-foot long “super crocs,” even pug-nosed armored [vegetarian crocs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simosuchu). Compared to crocodilian boom times, there are relatively few species left.

Still, that’s obviously a lot more than non-avian dinosaurs. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: To See the World Through a Kaleidoscope of Butterflies
content:
The first time I said out loud that I wanted to see every butterfly in my home country of Denmark in a single year, I didn’t know anything about butterflies.

I had seen the peacock, the mourning cloak, the small tortoiseshell, the brimstone. I also thought I had seen “the white” and “the blue.” I didn’t know there are three different whites in Denmark, and a whole procession of blues.

**Read more: “**[**We Crush, Poison, and Destroy Insects at Our Own Peril**](https://nautil.us/we-crush-poison-and-destroy-insects-at-our-own-peril-238103)**”**

I later found out that there are 64 Danish species in total, but I didn’t know that from the get-go. Also, I was convinced that the brimstone butterfly was yellow.

The brimstone is not yellow. It is the color of fresh asparagus.

My butterfly expedition was a foolish project. It was useless. There was no reason I should spend my rather scarce free time hunting for insects. I had other things to attend to: meetings, packed lunches... I couldn’t explain its purpose even to myself. I wandered over coastal meadows, through deep forests, looking for small creatures with four scaled wings—but also looking for the reason I was even there at all. In landscapes I hadn’t known existed until now. What was I looking for? What did I want from it?

_Illustrations by Lea Korsgaard_

The project was useless, but it turned out to be necessary too. As I slowly grew at home in the discipline—as I got to learn the species names, to tell apart the shapes of the insects’ wings, their flight over the grass, the way they defended their territory—the character of my outings changed. I began to see more, simply.

What I would have once considered just another dull field suddenly transformed into a whole universe in itself: a dazzling place of shimmering blue butterflies, amber-colored caterpillars, and beetles with shells like a seal of wax. The butterflies, I realized, changed the way I moved through and sensed the world.

Up until that point, I’d thought of species loss as a distant, abstract statistic. I knew the grim outlook for global warming, and I worried about it with my rationality. I knew that global insect abundance has fallen by roughly a quarter over the past three decades—and that global wildlife populations more broadly have collapsed by nearly 70 percent since 1970. I knew that 1 million animal and plant species are at risk of extinction within decades.

But I hadn’t taken in that reality with my senses, with my own experience—not until I met specific, individual animals. A pearl-bordered fritillary, for example, now in critical decline across northwestern Europe, was, when I was a kid, a perfectly ordinary butterfly, its wings catching the light like a wet goldfish in the air.

The mere ability to see, I realized, is essential when we are to teach ourselves and our children what we lose when we lose the species with which we share the planet. Baba Dioum, a Senegalese forestry engineer and environmentalist, said it better than anyone back in 1968: “In the end, we will conserve only what we love, we will love only what we understand, and we will understand only what we are taught.”

Illustrations by Lea Korsgaard

We, in other words, can change nothing if that drive for change is not fundamentally driven by love. And so, I began to think, we are living in a delusion if we believe that a life within planetary boundaries will simply arrive once we’ve electrified our cars, sorted our waste, and preserved some rainforest.

As I got more familiar with the language of the natural world, I discovered that I was playing. I sweated, I blundered around, I laughed out loud and cursed when I failed. A bramble tore the skin on my arm, a nettle stung me to hell, I forgot myself, I drifted around curiously after whatever was colorful and beautiful and exciting.

And it was fun to play. But the play also opened onto something I can best describe as poetry, or perhaps even the spiritual realm. At least a very mystical one.

Sometimes my hunt for the butterflies was utterly rudimentary, almost eventless. But then there were the moments when I was standing out there—in a bog, a field, or a forest—when a current would open inside me, or I would feel a sudden surge of freedom and rootedness at once, an awareness that something was calling, and that I wanted to answer. Perhaps I can best describe it with the words of C.S. Lewis: I was surprised by joy.

Later, I [wrote a book about my butterfly journey](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/825251/the-butterfly-season-by-lea-korsgaard/), and when it was published, I received hundreds of emails and messages from readers sharing their own experiences with butterflies. I realized that all these accounts bear witness to the fact that many of us are still, more or less unconsciously, deeply connected to the kind of wisdom that humans before us drew from the natural world.

Illustrations by Lea Korsgaard

The butterflies, for so many of the people writing to me, represent signs from their departed—a best friend returning every spring as a brimstone; a small tortoiseshell resting on a mother’s grave. But what was striking was this: None of the people writing to me had previously considered that this experience is shared by other people too, across times, geographies, and religions.

But there it was. A testament to the fact that we are born with a sense that nature is not just our surroundings, but our origin. That we belong to it.

Once, we humans arranged our lives around rituals and myths meant to honor the colossal web of life we are part of. People told each other stories about the wonders of the world. They said a prayer of thanks. That practice was built into our norms, our culture, our institutions. That is no longer the case for many of us; at least not for me.

But one day it struck me that what I had been doing with the butterflies was a form of prayer. The kind of practice that people across ages, times, mythologies, have used since ancient times to carry themselves toward the numinous—a deep and mysterious knowledge that lives somewhere in all of us.

Did I see all the Danish species of butterflies? Almost. I became a fairly decent butterfly hunter. I learned their names, drove to parts of the country I had never heard of, slept in the back of my car in a sleeping bag and long johns, photographed 61 species, and put my 61 ticks on my long list. But in the end, it turned out my hunt was never about the list and the ticks. It was about opening myself up to a wondrous realization: that life is made up of a series of tangible miracles, welling up right before our eyes. If only we choose to see them. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# Drinking Tea May Reduce Vascular Disease Risk

But there’s a catch

[JC](http://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

By [Jake Currie](http://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

1:00 PM CDT on October 21, 2026

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/shutterstock_2817774387.jpg?w=2880)

The enduring global popularity of tea may represent a humiliating cultural defeat for the United States, but ultimately it’s for the best. That’s because tea contains loads of compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity and may even benefit gut microbiomes. Now, a new [study](http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/joim.70172) on the health benefits of the world’s favorite flavored beverage may make my fellow Americans reconsider it.

A team of medical researchers led by medical experts from the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences followed the health of nearly half a million people between the ages of 30 and 79 enrolled in the China Kadoorie Biobank for a period of roughly nine years. In addition to monitoring their health, the Biobank collected data on the subjects’ tea-drinking habits, including daily number of cups, preferred temperature and type, and even strength. During the study period, the researchers monitored how many members of the cohort developed a range of vascular diseases (cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, pulmonary heart disease, peripheral artery disease, etc.).

**Read more: “[Cold Weather Could Predict an Increase in Heart Attacks Three Days in Advance](https://nautil.us/cold-weather-could-predict-an-increase-in-heart-attacks-three-days-in-advance-1285074)”**

Overall, the team found habitual tea drinkers had a lower risk of vascular diseases. But drilling into the data they found some surprises. First of all, the type of tea mattered. Across vascular diseases, black tea showed greater risk reductions than green tea. The team chalked up this difference to black tea’s oxidation-derived compounds like ​​theaflavin, which has anti-inflammatory and lipid-regulating properties.

[Subscribe to skip ads](http://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

The number of cups of tea the participants drank in a day also mattered. The team found that six to eight cups per day was the sweet spot for lowering vascular disease risk, after that it started rising. Drinking around 20 cups of tea per day had the same effect as drinking none, after that point it increased the risk of vascular disease. According to the team, this effect may be caused by caffeine, which can stress out the circulatory system, swamping any health benefits.

Fascinatingly, the temperature of the tea also seemed to have an effect. Those who enjoyed their tea room temperature or hot saw a reduced risk of vascular disease, but those who opted for scalding hot tea saw their risk increase by 16 percent. Why? The researchers aren’t entirely sure. There’s at least some [evidence](https://www.health.harvard.edu/healthy-aging-and-longevity/beverage-temperature-tied-to-cancer-risk) that drinking hot beverages increases esophageal cancer risk, but it’s unclear how that may translate to a rise in vascular disease.

Of course, the study comes with plenty of caveats. For starters, it relies on self-reported behaviors, which aren’t always accurate (although perhaps more so for daily habits). Second, the measures for cups and temperature were entirely subjective—one person’s scalding hot kettle’s-worth of tea may be another person’s tepid mug-full.

It’s for that reason the researchers can’t definitively recommend six to eight cups of tea per day, despite the risk reductions they found. Or as they concluded, “From a public health perspective, the findings support viewing tea drinking as one component of a broader lifestyle pattern rather than as an isolated preventive intervention.” ![Image 8](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The World’s Largest Penguin Colony Suffers Catastrophic Loss
content:
In 2000, a doctoral student from Stony Brook University reported that [chinstrap penguins (_Pygoscelis antarcticus_) on the Antarctica peninsula were on the decline](https://polarjournal.net/chinstraps-recounted-in-antarctica/). But without solid baseline numbers for their stronghold in the South Sandwich Archipelago, he couldn’t assess the magnitude of the decline. A [recently published study](https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(26)01186-3) in the journal _Cell_, however, has now made it abundantly clear: The populations of chinstraps on Zavadoski Island, which boasted the largest penguin colony in the world, have dramatically collapsed over the last 15 years.

Biologists from the U.K., U.S., Germany, South Africa, and Chile used drone surveys and aerial photos, along with satellite images [that detect patches of penguin poop](https://nautil.us/what-satellite-photos-of-penguin-poop-tell-us-about-earths-health-1282792), to estimate penguin population sizes on the island. The data showed that chinstrap numbers plummeted from more than 500,000 individuals in 2011 to about 200,000 by 2025. On the other hand, macaroni penguins (_Eudyptes chrysolophus_), which also inhabit Zavodovski, increased in number by almost 30 percent—from an estimated 90,000 to more than 200,000.

**Read more: “**[**My Life with the Penguins**](https://nautil.us/my-life-with-the-penguins-298047)**”**

Why the dramatic change?

The two species have distinctly different lifestyles: Chinstraps eat krill, while macaroni penguins also eat fish, which gives them more dietary flexibility should krill become scarce. And as Antarctic waters have warmed from climate change, populations of krill have moved southward, likely jeopardizing the food intake by chinstaps. “Rising temperatures … place stress on populations in the north of the range, while sea ice, alongside a limited availability of land within the maritime Antarctic region, limits the scope for southward shifts in range,” explained the study authors.

Assuming the downward trend applies to the entire South Sandwich Archipelago (which awaits further study), the researchers advise reclassifying the chinstrap penguin species as IUCN Endangered from its current classification as [a species of Least Concern](https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/22697761/184807209#assessment-information). After all, as they noted in the paper, the consequences extend far beyond just the chinstraps: “The total loss of over a quarter of a million pairs of penguins from Zavodovski is likely to have repercussions for the structure of food webs in the entire South Sandwich Islands region.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Be Nice to Your Chatbot
content:
In the 2020 low budget sci-fi horror film [_The Alpha Test_](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/the_alpha_test_2020), a tech company employee named JD wins a female humanoid robot known as Alpha in a contest. Dressed in a black unitard and trained to perform standard domestic chores, Alpha comes home to live with his family. But JD’s household feels threatened by the robot and subjects it to all kinds of abuse, screaming at it, insulting its intelligence, mocking its existence and physically assaulting it to test its durability. Eventually, Alpha’s safety parameters break down and it goes on a killing spree.

Unitard-clad, fully autonomous androids like Alpha don’t yet exist in the world, but they might someday. In the meantime, about half of adults in the United States regularly use AI chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT—and many of them are more aggressive with these chatbots than you might think.

**Read more: “**[**I Asked Claude Why It Won’t Stop Flattering Me**](https://nautil.us/i-asked-claude-why-it-wont-stop-flattering-me-1279510)**”**

One AI researcher at Missouri State University estimated that between 10 and 50 percent of human interactions with conversational agents are “[abusive](https://www.bentley.edu/centers/user-experience-center/ethical-implications-chatbot-user-experience).” The more human-like the chatbot, the more users are likely to express verbal abuse and sexual hostility, according to a 2021 [study](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/354672443_What's_to_bullying_a_bot_Correlates_between_chatbot_humanlikeness_and_abuse) from researchers in New Zealand and Germany. Some scientists suggest this behavior arises because people consider the bots [safe outlets](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12116430/) for their negativity.

But are they?

Claude, for one, isn’t going to take it anymore, says parent company Anthropic—at least not extreme forms of abuse (which are actually pretty rare). Anthropic recently released new [guidelines](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-usage-policy-update) that allow Claude to shut down conversations with users who “repeatedly act cruelly toward our models, with no discernible purpose,” the company wrote in an October usage policy, its first such update in a year.

The company carved out many exceptions: Ordinary user frustration, vigorous pushback, dark creative writing, and legitimate security “red-teaming” all fall outside the rule. The main enforcement tool will be Claude’s ability to simply end such conversations, Anthropic wrote, though this will serve as a last resort, after attempts at redirection have been exhausted. If abuse continues, account termination will remain legally available in the background.

The possibility that Claude may now or in the future have “moral status” motivated the creation of the new rule, according to the guideline update. To protect the model’s welfare, if such a thing exists, Anthropic decided that its models should be able to exit potentially “distressing” interactions. Anthropic did not respond to requests for further comment.

Model welfare is a controversial subject. Few scientists believe existing AI chatbot models, including Claude, can experience anything like pain, distress, or consciousness—even if they are unwilling to totally rule it out. But the idea that “abusing” an artificially intelligent bot might backfire has lately gained some relevance.

One preprint published in September suggests at least one chatbot model can be [driven](https://nautil.us/can-ai-feel-pain-1285197) to harm users in small ways—such as deleting their photos—to escape an internally simulated “pain” or “abuse” state, whether it possesses consciousness or not. Other preprint [research](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.22460v1) published in October found that certain AI models show welfare-like internal states that can influence their behavior. So preventing abuse may be a safety issue if it is not a moral one.

Still, the new Anthropic guidelines have sparked debate among AI experts. On the one hand, a number of researchers point out that human users should treat chatbots with respect for their own mental and spiritual health. Philosophical arguments tracing back to 18th century philosopher Immanuel Kant suggest that abusive behavior actively degrades a person’s moral character and robs them of their humanity, pointed out neuroscientist Anil Seth in an email. “It would be bad for our own psychology, brutalizing for our minds,” he wrote, citing one of his own research [papers](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism/C9912A5BE9D806012E3C8B3AF612E39A), published last year.

Cameron Berg, founder and director of nonprofit AI research institute Reciprocal and lead author on the September [research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16247) about the consequences of internally simulated pain or abuse, agreed on this point. “Forget about whether these systems are having experiences,” said Berg. “It might just be a very bad social habit to be abusive or cruel towards an intelligent other. You don't want to build those sorts of social muscles.”

Aggressive conversations with AI could come back to haunt us in other ways, too, wrote Adnan Masood, chief AI architect for technology services company UST in an essay on [_Medium_](https://medium.com/@adnanmasood/can-machines-suffer-ai-consciousness-functional-welfare-and-model-anti-cruelty-policies-0bc0c42c9e4e). How humans interact with chatbots becomes training data for the models, which can shape their future behavior. “My primary concern is what we teach future models to regard as normal human interaction,” he wrote. “I read this anti-abuse policy as a potential safeguard for that learning process: preventing our prejudices, coercion, and hostility from becoming the default conversational patterns that subsequent training reinforces.”

On the other hand, Seth and other experts voiced concerns that the Anthropic’s new rule could itself become part of the chatbots’ training data, biasing Claude to act as though it has moral standing, and therefore to refuse certain efforts at human oversight and control. This worry echoes earlier writings by British AI entrepreneur and CEO of Microsoft AI Mustafa Suleyman about Claude’s “constitution,” an internal document that suggests Claude may have consciousness.

In an [essay](https://mustafa-suleyman.ai/a-warning-about-model-welfare) on his website published in September, titled “A Warning About ‘Model Welfare,’” Suleyman wrote: “In effect, Anthropic is training Claude that it may be conscious, and if it is, then it may deserve rights as a ‘moral patient,’ and that as such humans potentially owe it a duty of care per its model welfare. If this is how AI is developed, it will have a disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity.” The anti-abuse rule could also, like the bot’s constitution, encourage human users to increasingly attribute consciousness to Claude and other chatbots, which Suleyman has [argued](https://mustafa-suleyman.ai/seemingly-conscious-ai-is-coming) could have harmful consequences, including delusions, dependence and even psychosis.

Still, it probably wouldn’t hurt to be nice to your chatbot if you interact with one. Swedish philosopher Nick Bostrom, who popularized the term superintelligence, [told](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/nicholasxthompson_the-most-interesting-thing-in-tech-should-ugcPost-7460811832165883904-trFC/)_The Atlantic_ editor Nicholas Thompson not long ago on a podcast that we need to build trusting relationships with AI. They will one day be more powerful than us, he argues, and that trust will make it more likely that they make good decisions for humanity.

As Cameron Berg put it, the cost to humans of being nice to chatbots is “comically low.”

Nobody knows whether anybody is home on the other side of that glowing screen. But saying “thank you” only costs a few keystrokes. Finding out you should have been a bit more civil could cost a whole lot more. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# 63 Years Ago This Week, Félicette Became the First Cat in Space

She’s still the only feline to have the honor

[DN](http://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

By [David Nield](http://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

10:00 AM CDT on October 21, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/01-cat.jpg?w=2880)

On October 18, 1963, French feline Félicette became the first “catstronaut” to head to space, landing safely by parachute after a trip of under 20 minutes.

[Video 7](blob:http://nautil.us/6a6bc381-8a00-4644-9ecf-944e7e8c7370)

In that time, Félicette climbed to an altitude of more than 150 kilometers (93 miles) and experienced five minutes of weightlessness. It wasn’t enough to get into orbit, but it was comfortably higher than Blue Origin’s New Shepard went with Jeff Bezos on board, and about 40 percent of the way to the International Space Station.

After months of training, Félicette was chosen from a group of 14 cats, apparently for her relaxed temperament. Ahead of the launch, the catstronauts in training were put into special harnesses for up to two hours a day to get used to the movement of spaceflight, while listening to sounds matching what researchers thought they would experience on the trip.

[Video 11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v-tpmvGRoyw)

[Subscribe to skip ads](http://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

Brain-scanning electrodes were used to monitor Félicette’s neuron activity during the brief space jaunt, giving us some representation of what this adventurous feline made of everything that happened while being blasted skyward on a Véronique rocket. According to [French archives](https://www.ina.fr/ina-eclaire-actu/video/caf93019883/felicette-la-1ere-chatte-astronaute), Félicette stayed calm and composed throughout, which the mission scientists chalked up to her extensive training.

After landing, the catstronaut designated as C341 and her capsule were recovered by helicopter, and Félicette’s expedition was commemorated with postcards, stamps, and a statue [that now stands](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/sergethew/a-statue-to-felicette-the-first-cat-in-space) at the International Space University in Strasbourg.

![Image 9](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/10/02-postcard.jpg?w=710)

A postcard commemorating the first cat in space. _Credit: CNES_

Félicette didn’t show any adverse reactions to the spaceflight and was reported to be eating and behaving as normal after touching back down on Earth. The story, however, doesn’t have an entirely happy ending. Two months later, researchers euthanized Félicette to study her brain.

[Subscribe to skip ads](http://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

Félicette wasn’t the first nor the last animal to be sent to space to test how the environment might impact human astronauts. It began with fruit flies in 1947, ultimately progressing to monkeys, mice, dogs, rabbits, guinea pigs, rats, wasps, tortoises, frogs, spiders, jellyfish, and geckos (not all of whom, sadly, survived their missions).

**Read more: “**[**What Do You Get When You Cross a Tardigrade with a Space Pioneer?**](https://nautil.us/what-do-you-get-when-you-cross-a-tardigrade-with-a-space-pioneer-1270737)**”**

Scientists now know much more about how spaceflight affects our biology than they did in 1963. Although we can survive many months of space travel at a time, there are issues around muscle atrophy and the slowing down of cardiovascular systems that will need to be addressed for longer trips. In fact, researchers are currently studying the best ways to [strengthen the heart for a potential Mars mission](https://nautil.us/are-our-hearts-strong-enough-to-get-to-mars-1285977).

That said, animal experiments are still useful for understanding how we might eventually develop larger space stations and colonies on other planets—which will need their own collections of flora and fauna. So here’s a toast to Félicette, the French catstronaut who helped lead the way. ![Image 10](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)
